chapter.name: Minerals and Energy Resources
chapter.blurb: What a mineral is, how geologists classify minerals and the five ways they occur; India's ferrous, non-ferrous and non-metallic minerals and where each is mined; the health and environmental hazards of mining and why mineral resources must be conserved; India's conventional energy sources (coal, petroleum, natural gas, electricity) and non-conventional ones (nuclear, solar, wind, biogas, tidal, geothermal); and why energy, like minerals, is finite and must be used judiciously.

concepts.name: Minerals: meaning, classification and mode of occurrence
concepts.description: What a mineral is, how geologists classify minerals for general and commercial purposes (Fig. 5.1), and the five distinct ways minerals occur in nature.
concepts.idea: A mineral is a naturally occurring, homogenous substance with a definable internal structure, and for general and commercial purposes minerals are classified as metallic (ferrous, non-ferrous and precious), non-metallic, and energy minerals, each occurring in one of five characteristic ways.
concepts.rule: Geologists define a mineral as a homogenous, naturally occurring substance with a definable internal structure. Minerals occur in 'ores', an accumulation of a mineral mixed with other elements concentrated enough to be commercially viable to extract. Fig. 5.1 classifies minerals as Metallic (Ferrous, e.g. iron ore and manganese; Non-Ferrous, e.g. copper, lead, tin and bauxite; and Precious, e.g. gold, silver and platinum), Non-Metallic (e.g. mica, salt, potash, sulphur, granite, limestone, marble and sandstone), and Energy Minerals (coal, petroleum and natural gas). Minerals occur in five main forms: (i) veins and lodes in the cracks, crevices, faults or joints of igneous and metamorphic rocks; (ii) beds or layers in sedimentary rocks, formed by deposition, accumulation and concentration in horizontal strata, or by evaporation; (iii) a residual mass of weathered material left after the decomposition of surface rocks and the removal of soluble constituents, which is how bauxite forms; (iv) placer deposits, alluvial deposits in the sands of valley floors and the base of hills; and (v) dissolved in ocean waters, or as manganese nodules on ocean beds.
concepts.example: Major metallic minerals like tin, copper, zinc and lead are obtained from veins and lodes formed when minerals in liquid or gaseous form are forced upward through cavities and cool as they rise; bauxite, by contrast, forms when surface rocks decompose and their soluble parts wash away, leaving a residual mass behind.

questions.q: Explain, using this chapter, why the same element -- for example iron -- can appear in more than one of the classes in Fig. 5.1's classification of minerals, and why manganese nodules on the ocean bed illustrate that mode of occurrence and mineral class are two separate ideas.
questions.a: Fig. 5.1 classifies minerals like iron ore under Ferrous, a composition-based class, which says nothing about how or where the mineral occurs. Mode of occurrence is a separate idea about the physical process and location of formation, such as veins and lodes or ocean beds. Manganese nodules show this clearly: manganese is classified as a ferrous metallic mineral in Fig. 5.1, yet this particular occurrence of it forms on the ocean bed, one of the five modes of occurrence, which is a completely different kind of fact about it. The same mineral can therefore be described both by which class it belongs to and by how it happens to occur in a given deposit, and the two descriptions do not have to match any pattern.
s: Explains that Fig. 5.1's classes describe composition, not location or process of formation

concepts.name: Ferrous minerals: iron ore and manganese
concepts.description: Iron ore (magnetite and hematite) and manganese: their properties, uses, and where each is mined in India.
concepts.idea: Ferrous minerals, which contain iron, account for about three-fourths of the value of India's metallic mineral production, and this chapter surveys iron ore (magnetite and hematite) and manganese.
concepts.rule: Magnetite is the finest iron ore, with up to 70 per cent iron content and excellent magnetic qualities valuable in the electrical industry. Hematite is the most important industrial iron ore by quantity used, with a slightly lower iron content of 50-60 per cent. In 2018-19 almost the entire production of iron ore (97 per cent) came from Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka and Jharkhand. India's four major iron ore belts are: the Odisha-Jharkhand belt (Badampahar mines in Mayurbhanj and Kendujhar districts, Odisha; Gua and Noamundi in Singhbhum district, Jharkhand); the Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur belt (the Bailadila range in Bastar district, Chhattisgarh, exported via Vishakhapatnam to Japan and South Korea); the Ballari-Chitradurga-Chikkamagaluru-Tumakuru belt (the Kudremukh mines in Karnataka, a 100 per cent export unit, ore piped as slurry to a port near Mangaluru); and the Maharashtra-Goa belt (exported through Marmagao port). Manganese is mainly used in manufacturing steel and ferro-manganese alloy (about 10 kg of manganese per tonne of steel), and also in bleaching powder, insecticides and paints; in 2018-19 Madhya Pradesh (33%), Maharashtra (27%), Odisha (16%), Karnataka (12%) and Andhra Pradesh (10%) were its leading producers.
concepts.example: The Bailadila hills in the Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur belt are named for their resemblance to the hump of an ox, while the highest peak in the Western Ghats near the Kudremukh mines is named for resembling a horse's face, since 'Kudre' means horse in Kannada.

concepts.name: Non-ferrous minerals: copper and bauxite
concepts.description: Copper and bauxite: their properties, uses, and where each is mined in India, and India's contrasting position in the two.
concepts.idea: India is critically deficient in copper but is a significant producer of bauxite, the ore from which aluminium is obtained.
concepts.rule: Copper is malleable, ductile and a good conductor, mainly used in electrical cables, electronics and chemical industries; the Balaghat mines (Madhya Pradesh), Khetri mines (Rajasthan) and Singhbhum district (Jharkhand) are its leading producers, though India is critically deficient in copper reserves and production. Bauxite, a clay-like substance, is formed by the decomposition of rocks rich in aluminium silicates, and it is from bauxite that alumina and then aluminium is obtained; aluminium combines the strength of metals like iron with extreme lightness, good conductivity and great malleability. India's bauxite deposits are mainly in the Amarkantak plateau, the Maikal hills and the Bilaspur-Katni plateau region; Odisha was the largest bauxite producer in 2018-19, with the Panchpatmali deposits in Koraput district its most important.
concepts.example: In 2018-19 Odisha alone produced 65 per cent of India's bauxite, while Jharkhand (10%), Gujarat (9%), Chhattisgarh (6%), Maharashtra (6%) and Madhya Pradesh (3%) shared most of the rest.

concepts.name: Conventional sources of energy: coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity
concepts.description: India's main conventional energy sources: how coal and petroleum form and occur, where India's natural gas reserves and pipelines are, and how electricity is generated.
concepts.idea: Energy resources are classified as conventional (firewood, cattle dung cake, coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity) and non-conventional, and this chapter surveys India's main conventional sources in turn: coal, petroleum, natural gas and electricity.
concepts.rule: Coal, India's most abundant fossil fuel, forms by compression of plant material and occurs in grades depending on burial depth and time -- peat (low carbon, high moisture), lignite (soft, high moisture, chiefly at Neyveli, Tamil Nadu), bituminous (the most popular commercial coal; metallurgical coal is high grade bituminous used for smelting iron) and anthracite (the highest quality hard coal) -- occurring in Gondwana rock (about 200 million years old, giving metallurgical coal in the Damodar Valley's Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro fields, and the Godavari, Mahanadi, Son and Wardha valleys) and Tertiary rock (about 55 million years old, in Meghalaya, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland); because coal is bulky and loses weight as it is used, heavy industry and thermal power stations locate near coalfields. Petroleum occurs mainly in anticlines and fault traps of tertiary-age rock, trapped in a porous oil-bearing layer between non-porous layers with gas, being lighter, above the oil; Mumbai High, Gujarat (led by Ankleshwar) and Assam (India's oldest oil-producing state, with the Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran-Hugrijan fields) are the major producing areas. Natural gas, released alongside crude oil, serves as a fuel for power, industry, transport (CNG) and cooking (PNG); its major reserves are in the Mumbai High/Cambay basin area and, more recently, the Krishna-Godavari basin, linked since the HVJ pipeline by GAIL (India) into a growing cross-country gas grid. Electricity is generated either from fast-flowing water (hydroelectricity, a renewable resource, as at Bhakra Nangal, the Damodar Valley Corporation and the Kopili Hydel Project) or by burning coal, petroleum or natural gas (thermal power, from non-renewable fossil fuels); once generated, the electricity is exactly the same either way.

concepts.idea: Rising fossil-fuel dependence and its environmental costs make non-conventional, largely renewable sources -- nuclear, solar, wind, biogas, tidal and geothermal -- an increasingly important part of India's energy mix.
concepts.rule: Nuclear or atomic energy, obtained by altering the structure of atoms, uses Uranium and Thorium (found in Jharkhand and the Aravalli ranges of Rajasthan, and Thorium also in Kerala's Monazite sands) across six nuclear power stations. Wind power's largest cluster runs from Nagarcoil to Madurai in Tamil Nadu, with other farms in Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Gujarat, Kerala, Maharashtra and Lakshadweep; Nagarcoil and Jaisalmer are named for effective use. Biogas, made from shrubs, farm waste and animal or human waste, has higher thermal efficiency than kerosene, dung cake or charcoal, and cattle-dung 'Gobar gas plants' give farmers both energy and improved manure. Tidal energy uses floodgate dams across inlets, trapping high-tide water to drive turbines as it flows back to sea; the Gulf of Khambhat, the Gulf of Kuchchh and the Sunderban delta offer ideal conditions. Geothermal energy taps heat from the earth's interior, where a high geothermal gradient heats groundwater into steam that drives turbines; India has two experimental projects, at Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh) and the Puga Valley (Ladakh).
